THE POWER
BEHIND PROGRESS

THE POWER
BEHIND PROGRESS
Progress needs power, and power needs capital. For nearly four 
decades, PFC has provided it, financing the generation, transmission and 
distribution that carried India from chronic shortage to surplus. Set up 
in 1986 to fund the nation's power sector, we have grown into its largest 
power sector financier and its largest renewable financier, with capital 
reaching every stage of the value chain and the infrastructure around it.
Today, India is building a new energy economy. Non-fossil sources have 
crossed half the country's installed capacity, five years ahead of target, 
and the decade ahead calls for financing on an unprecedented scale.  
This is the ground we are built for. We fund the transition  
end-to-end: generation, transmission, storage, distribution reform and 
green hydrogen, with discipline, scale and purpose.
Behind every megawatt added and every grid strengthened is the capital 
that makes it possible. That is the power behind progress.
Cover Narration
This year's cover carries the theme forward: PFC as the power behind India's progress. It reads as a current of energy and capital 
moving through the nation, from the natural forces that generate power to the grids, cities and communities it reaches. A single 
source sends light outward, tracing how finance becomes electricity and electricity becomes growth. The visual holds PFC at 
the centre of India's energy transition, the steady force that funds generation, carries it across the country, and turns national 
ambition into infrastructure that lasts.

About PFC
The Nation's Power Financier
Power Finance Corporation Limited 
(PFC) is a Schedule-A Maharatna CPSE 
under the Ministry of Power and the 
largest government-owned NBFC in 
India. We were set up in 1986 to finance 
the country's power sector, and across 
the four decades since, we have funded 
generation, transmission and distribution 
capacity nationwide.
We are the nodal agency for several of the government's 
principal power programmes, among them the 
Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), the 
Ultra Mega Power Projects (UMPPs) and the Integrated 
Power Development Scheme (IPDS), and the Bid Process 
Coordinator for Independent Transmission Projects 
(ITPs). These mandates place us at the centre of the 
sector's reform agenda.
Our lending covers rupee term loans, short-term 
finance, lease financing and transitional funding. 
Beyond the power sector, we now finance e-mobility 
and charging infrastructure, roads, ports, metro rail 
and smart cities, widening our book as the country's 
infrastructure needs grow.
We lend to central and state utilities, power equipment 
manufacturers, government departments and large 
infrastructure developers.
PFC is the highest profit-making NBFC in India and the 
country's largest renewable energy financier, carrying 
a 'AAA' domestic credit rating and an international 
rating at par with India's sovereign. We rank #33 on 
the Fortune 500 India (December 2025) and #18 on 
the Forbes Global 2000: India list (2025). As the first 
Maharatna from the financial sector, we have helped 
finance close to half of India's installed power capacity.
Our Vision
To be the leading institutional partner for the power and allied infrastructure sectors 
in India and overseas across the value chain.
Our Mission
PFC would be the most preferred financial institution, providing affordable and 
competitive products and services with efficient and internationally integrated 
sourcing and servicing, partnering in the reforms in the Indian power sector and 
enhancing value to its stakeholders by promoting efficient investments in the power 
and allied sectors in India and abroad.
We will achieve this by being a dynamic, flexible, forward-looking, trustworthy, 
socially responsible organisation, sensitive to our stakeholders' interests, profitable 
and sustainable at all times, with transparency and integrity in operations.

PFC Consulting Limited, our wholly owned subsidiary, 
offers specialised advisory services spanning 
transaction advisory and project development, 
built around the changing requirements of India's

PFC Infra Finance IFSC Ltd. (PIFIL)
Incorporated on 11 February 2024, PIFIL was the first 
finance company set up by a government-owned NBFC 
at the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) in 
GIFT City, Gujarat. It funds infrastructure projects with 
a particular focus on renewable energy, drawing on 
the global capital and expertise available at IFSC. The 
platform widens our international footprint and brings 
efficient financing within reach of a broader client base.
REC Ltd.
REC Limited, a key member of the PFC Group, is a 
registered infrastructure finance company that funds 
and supports power sector projects across India.
Ultra Mega Power Projects
The Government of India's Ultra Mega Power 
Project (UMPP) initiative supports the development 
of large-scale power projects. Through dedicated 
special purpose vehicles, we secure the necessary 
clearances, acquire land and water, and arrange coal 
linkages, readying each project for faster execution 
by developers.

projects, pumped hydro storage and battery energy

ammonia co-firing, flue gas desulphurisation (FGD) and 
thermal plants, alongside nuclear power projects.

A Decade of Capital 
Formation
The targets translate into one of the largest financing 
requirements in any infrastructure market, and it 
falls almost entirely within the segments we lend to. 
The National Electricity Plan 2022-32 puts generation 
investment alone at close to I33 lakh crore by 2032, 
with a further I9.15 lakh crore needed in transmission 
to carry 500 GW of renewable capacity to the grid. 
Storage adds another layer, with 47 GW of battery and 
around 31 GW of pumped storage planned alongside 
renewables. Distribution, meanwhile, remains the 
sector's weakest link financially, the very area the 
government's reform programme, and our role as its 
nodal agency, is built to strengthen.
For PFC, this is the shape of the 
opportunity ahead. Generation, 
transmission, storage, distribution 
reform and green hydrogen are 
not new frontiers for us; this is 
already the core of our book. 
As India's largest power sector 
financier and its largest renewable 
financier, we are positioned to fund 
the transition end to end and the 
decade of capital formation now 
underway is, in large part, a decade 
of lending we are built for.

Alongside this, the National Green Hydrogen Mission, 
the promotion of Battery Energy Storage Systems 
(BESS), pumped storage projects, transmission and 
other emerging technologies are laying the foundation 
for a resilient, flexible and low-carbon energy system. 
The coming decade will witness one of the largest 
infrastructure investment cycles in India's history. 
As per the Draft National Electricity Policy 2026, 
investments of H50 lakh crore are required across 
generation, transmission, distribution and energy 
storage by 2032. This represents one of the largest 
infrastructure investment opportunities anywhere in 
the world. 
Financing India's Energy Transition
Yet, the defining challenge before us is not merely 
technological; it is financial.
Such a transformation cannot be financed through 
short-term capital alone. It requires institutions capable 
of mobilising patient capital, managing long-gestation 
infrastructure risks and supporting investments that 
will create value over several decades.
Four Decades of Nation Building
For forty years, Power Finance Corporation has fulfilled 
precisely this role.
Established to strengthen India's power sector, PFC 
has evolved alongside the nation's changing priorities. 
From financing conventional power generation and 
transmission projects in its early years to supporting 
renewable energy, transmission corridors, energy 
storage, distribution reforms and emerging clean 
- energy technologies today, PFC has consistently 
adapted to the evolving needs of the sector while 
remaining true to its core purpose - to provide long-
term financial support for projects that are critical to 
India's development.
As the nodal agency for the Revamped Distribution 
Sector Scheme (RDSS), PFC has played a critical role 
in strengthening the India's distribution sector by 
enabling investments in smart metering, infrastructure 
modernisation and operational efficiency. A strong and 
financially sustainable distribution sector remains the 
cornerstone of a resilient power system and will be 
critical to sustaining India's long-term energy security 
and economic growth.
With four decades of experience, PFC remains 
uniquely positioned to mobilise long-term capital, 
develop innovative financing solutions and partner 
with stakeholders in building India's future 
power ecosystem.
Delivering Performance with Purpose
The opportunities before India are unprecedented, 
but so are the responsibilities entrusted to institutions 
like PFC. 
During FY 2025-26, PFC continued to be 
India's highest profit-making NBFC, while 
the PFC Group reaffirmed its leadership 
as India's largest NBFC Group with a 
consolidated balance sheet of around J12 
lakh crore.

Our performance during FY 2025–26 reflects not only 
strong financial outcomes but also our continued ability 
to anticipate the evolving needs of the sector and 
respond with discipline, agility and purpose.
Against a backdrop of global geopolitical volatility 
and evolving financial markets, India continued to 
demonstrate remarkable economic resilience. Policy 
continuity sustained public capital expenditure and 
robust infrastructure development created significant 
opportunities across the power sector value chain. 
PFC remained well positioned to capitalise on 
this momentum while maintaining its unwavering 
commitment to financial prudence and long-term 
value creation.
During FY 2025-26, PFC continued to be India's highest 
profit-making NBFC, while the PFC Group reaffirmed 
its leadership as India's largest NBFC Group with a 
consolidated balance sheet of around H12 lakh crore.
On a consolidated basis, profit after tax increased to 
H33,625 crore, while standalone Profit After Tax crossed 
H20,000 crore for the first time, reaching H20,051 crore. 
Standalone net worth surpassed the landmark H1 lakh 
crore, significantly enhancing our capacity to finance 
India's growing infrastructure requirements.
Also, during FY 2025–26, we recorded annual 
disbursements of approximately H1.65 lakh crore, while 
our loan assets expanded to H5.80 lakh crore, with 
H90,135 crore of renewable book. Even as we grew, we 
maintained a healthy Capital Adequacy Ratio of 23.44%, 
ensuring that our growth continues to be supported by 
a strong capital base.
The Board has recommended a dividend of H18.55 per 
share, the highest in the Company's history, reflecting 
our commitment to delivering sustainable value to our 
shareholders while preserving financial strength for 
future growth.
Recognising the increasing importance of sustainable 
finance, we have continued to strengthen our 
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) framework 
and integrate sustainability considerations into our 
financing strategy. Our objective is not merely to finance 
growth, but to finance growth responsibly, balancing 
commercial excellence with environmental stewardship 
and long-term societal impact.
During the year, we also expanded our engagement with 
leading international development finance institutions, 
including Japan Bank for International Cooperation 
(JBIC) and Export Finance Australia (EFA), broadening 
access to diversified sources of long-term capital and 
reinforcing PFC's standing in global financial market.
The proposed merger of REC Limited 
with PFC represents much more than 
the coming together of two successful 
institutions. It is a strategic step towards 
strengthening India's development 
finance landscape.

FY 2025–26 also marked one of the most significant 
strategic developments in PFC's history.
The proposed merger of REC Limited with PFC 
represents much more than the coming together of 
two successful institutions. It is a strategic step towards 
strengthening India's development finance landscape.
Upon completion, the merged entity will create one 
of India's largest specialised infrastructure financing 
institutions, with an aggregate loan book of around 
H12 lakh crore. The combined scale will strengthen 
our ability to mobilise larger pools of domestic and 
international capital, diversify funding sources and 
finance increasingly complex infrastructure projects 
across the evolving value chain. 
For borrowers, this will mean stronger and innovative 
financing capabilities. For investors, it offers enhanced 
operational efficiencies and long-term value creation. 
For the nation, it strengthens an institution capable of 
supporting one of the world's most ambitious energy 
transition and infrastructure investment programmes.
This is not simply an organisational milestone; 
it is an opportunity to build an institution that is 
better equipped to support India's next phase of 
economic growth.
Growth Anchored in Prudence
While our scale continues to expand, our philosophy 
remains unchanged.
Sustainable growth is founded on sound governance, 
prudent risk management, disciplined capital allocation 
and financial resilience. We believe that long-term 
shareholder value is created not by taking greater risks, 
but by managing them better.
These principles have guided PFC for four decades 
and will continue to remain the cornerstone of our 
growth strategy.
Looking Ahead
As we enter our fifth decade, we do so with a clear 
conviction: our role is no longer limited to financing 
power projects. Our responsibility is to help finance 
India's energy future.
Sustainable growth is founded on sound 
governance, prudent risk management, 
disciplined capital allocation and financial 
resilience. Long-term shareholder value is 
created not by taking greater risks but by 
managing them better.

("TDS") from the dividend payable to its shareholders 
at the rates prescribed under the Income-tax Act, 
2025 and the rules made thereunder.

residential status of the shareholder, the category of 
the shareholder, availability of Permanent Account 
Number (PAN), and the declarations, forms and 
other documents submitted by the shareholder in 
accordance with the provisions of the Income-tax 
Act, 2025. Certain categories of shareholders, such 
as Mutual Funds, Insurance Companies and other 
entities specifically exempt under the provisions 
of the Income-tax Act, 2025, may be eligible for 
exemption or deduction of tax at a concessional 
rate subject to the submission of the prescribed 
declarations and supporting documents. In the case 
of non-resident shareholders, including Foreign 
Portfolio Investors (FPIs) and Foreign Institutional 
Investors (FIIs), tax shall be deducted at the rates 
prescribed under the Income-tax Act, 2025 or at the 
beneficial rate available under the applicable Double 
Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA), subject 
to the fulfilment of the prescribed conditions and 
submission of the requisite documents.
	
To enable the Company to determine the correct 
rate of TDS, shareholders falling under specified 
categories, including Mutual Funds, Insurance 
Companies, Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), 
Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs), Foreign Portfolio 
Investors (FPIs) and other eligible shareholders, are 
required to furnish the prescribed declarations, 
certificates, forms and supporting documents 
(including, wherever applicable, PAN, registration 
certificate, self-declaration, tax residency documents, 
declaration of beneficial ownership and such other 
documents as may be prescribed under the Income-
tax Act, 2025) within the timelines specified by 
the Company.

Insurance Companies, Mutual Funds and Alternative 
Investment Funds (AIFs) established in India, and 
Non-Resident Non-Individual Members, including

The following statement sets out the material facts 
relating to the special business mentioned in Item No.8 of 
the accompanying Notice:
As per Sec 180(1) (c) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Board 
of Directors of a public company, shall not, except with 
the consent of the shareholders by a special resolution, 
borrow money, where the moneys to be borrowed, 
together with the moneys already borrowed by the 
Company (apart from temporary loans obtained from the 
Company’s bankers in the ordinary course of business) will 
exceed the aggregate of paid-up capital of the Company, 
its free reserves and securities premium.
Accordingly, in the special resolution passed by the 
shareholders in the 34th Annual General Meeting of the 
Company held on September 29, 2020, the consent of 
the Company was accorded to the Board of Directors of 
the Company under the provisions of Section 180(1)(c) of 
Companies Act, 2013 to raise such sum or sums of money 
from time to time as may be required for the purpose of 
the business of the Company and/or as may be directed to 
raise on behalf of Ministry/Govt. of India, notwithstanding 
that the money to be borrowed together with the money 
already borrowed by the Company (apart from temporary 
loans as explained in Section 180(1)(c) of Companies Act, 
2013 obtained by the Company in the ordinary course 
of business)may, at any time, exceed up to sum of Rs. 
6,00,000 crore (Rupees six lakh crore only) from Indian 
Rupee borrowing and amount equivalent to USD 15 Billion 
(Fifteen Billion US Dollars only) in any foreign currency 
respectively over and above the aggregate paid up share 
capital of the Company and its free reserves (that is to say 
reserve not set apart for any specific purpose).
The fund requirement of the Company has been 
continuously increasing over the years, to meet the ever 
increasing demand of the power sector.
Thus, considering the Company’s projected funding 
requirements over next 4-5 years and to provide adequate 
flexibility for raising resources from International markets, 
the Board in its Meeting held on July 23, 2026, accorded 
approval for seeking the approval of shareholders for 
enhancing the borrowing limit under section 180(1)(c) 
of the Companies Act 2013 from Rs.6,00,000 crore to Rs. 
9,00,000 crore (Rupees nine lakh crore only) from Indian 
Rupee borrowing and to increase the foreign currency 
borrowing limit from USD 15 Billion to USD 25 Billion 
(Twenty Five Billion US Dollars only).
The Board further recommends the Resolution given at Sr. 
No. 8 of this notice for your approval as Special Resolution.

relatives do not have any concern or interest, financial or

PFC-REC merger
	
The Hon'ble Finance Minister, in the Union Budget 
for FY2026-27 proposed to restructure Power 
Finance Corporation and REC Limited in order to 
achieve scale and improve efficiency in the Public 
Sector NBFCs. Further, PFC's Board accorded its 
in-principle approval for the merger, subject to 
the merged entity continuing as a Government 
Company under the Companies Act, 2013.
	
Subsequently, the Board of both the Companies 
in their meeting held on 28.06.2026 approved the 
Scheme of merger, providing merger by absorption 
of REC into PFC with effect from the Appointed 
Date on a going concern basis and the consequent 
dissolution of REC without being wound up. The 
Eligible Shareholders of REC, as on the Record Date 
(to be notified) will get 88 equity shares of PFC of 
INR 10/- each fully paid up for every 100 equity shares 
of REC of INR 10/- each fully paid up in accordance 
with the share exchange ratio. The merger process 
is underway.
	
The scheme and other relevant documents are 
available on the websites of both the Companies.

LCR Compliance
	
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has prescribed 
the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) framework for 
NBFCs to ensure maintenance of an adequate 
liquidity buffer. The framework requires NBFCs to 
hold sufficient High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) to 
withstand any acute liquidity stress scenario for a 
period of 30 calendar days.
	
PFC is maintaining 100% of the required HQLA to 
cover the net cash outflows over the next 30 calendar 
days, in accordance with the RBI guidelines on LCR. 
As on March 31, 2026, the Company's HQLA stood 
at I3,349.05 crore, with an LCR ratio of 148.60%, 
demonstrating compliance with the applicable 
regulatory requirements.

11.	 Building Resilience: Our Multi-Layered Risk 
Approach
i.	
Asset Liability Management
	
Your Company has implemented a comprehensive 
and robust Asset Liability Management (ALM) 
Policy, aligned with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) 
guidelines. The policy is designed to ensure focused 
and proactive management of liquidity and interest 
rate risks as follows:
	
Risk Monitoring Methodologies:
	
1.	
Liquidity Risk: Monitored using the cash flow 
approach to assess the timing of cash inflows 
and outflows.
	
2.	
Interest Rate Risk: Measured through traditional 
gap analysis, as prescribed by the RBI guidelines.
	
Aforesaid analysis is made on periodical basis in 
various time buckets and is used for critical decisions 
regarding the time, volume and maturity profile of 
the borrowings and creation of mix of assets and 
liabilities in terms of time period (short, medium and 
long-term) and in terms of fixed and floating interest 
rates. The details of the asset liability management 
maturity pattern are given at Note No. 53.1 of the 
Notes to Accounts of the Standalone Financial 
statements forming part of this Annual Report.
ii.	
Foreign Currency Risk Management
	
The Company has established a comprehensive 
“Policy for Management of Risks on Foreign Currency 
Borrowings” to identify, assess, and mitigate risks 
arising from foreign currency exposures. In line with this 
framework, the Company actively manages exchange 
rate and interest rate risks associated with foreign 
currency borrowings through appropriate hedging 
instruments, including forwards, options, and swaps.
	
As at March 31, 2026, the Company’s total outstanding 
foreign currency liabilities stood at USD equivalent 
10,302 million, comprising borrowings denominated 
in USD 6,332 million, JPY 344,288 million, EUR 1,421 
million, and GBP 135 million. Out of the total foreign 
currency borrowing portfolio 97% is hedged i.e. USD 
eqv 10,027 mn. Also, 98% of the foreign currency 
portfolio with residual maturity up to 5 years is hedged.
iii.	 Information Security Risk Management
	
Information is an asset to PFC and Information Security 
(IS) solutions are implemented to protect these assets in 
order to achieve organisational goals. The purpose of the 
Information Security (IS) is to provide controlled access 
to sensitive information only to legitimate, authorised 
and authenticated users. With the implementation of 
Information Security & Risk Management mechanism 
the data Confidentiality, Integrity & Availability (CIA) 
is ensured through proactive risk assessments such 
as VAPT activities, Quarterly Risk Register review, 
regular patching, system updates, policy updates 
& implementation, SoPs, preventive maintenance 
activities, regular system reviews etc
iv.	 Integrated Enterprise Wide Risk Management
	
To effectively identify, assess, and mitigate risks, the 
Company has established an Integrated Enterprise-
Wide Risk Management Policy (IRM Policy). For 
the effective implementation and oversight of 
the policy, the Company has constituted a Risk 
Management Committee.
	
Under the IRM Policy, the Company has identified 
significant risk parameters arising from its business 
operations, business model, and the use of financial 
instruments. These parameters encompass a wide 
spectrum of risks, including operational, financial, market, 
and regulatory risks, among others. The identified risks 
are periodically assessed and monitored to ensure timely 
mitigation and effective risk management.
	
Further, the Company maintains a comprehensive 
risk register, which acts as a centralised repository 
of relevant information pertaining to identified risks, 
their potential impact, mitigation measures, and 
ongoing monitoring mechanisms.

i.	
Annual Integrated Rating of Power 
Distribution Utilities
	
As part of the power sector reform initiatives, the 
Ministry of Power has instituted an Integrated Rating 
Framework to assess the performance of power 
distribution utilities across the country. The primary 
objective of the Integrated Rating exercise is to grade 
all utilities in the power distribution sector based on 
their financial performance and their ability to sustain 
the performance over time. Private Distribution 
Utilities and Power Departments are also included to 
provide complete sectoral coverage.
	
The rating framework objectively evaluates the 
performance of distribution utilities across various 
parameters broadly classified under i) Financial 
Sustainability ii) Performance Excellence and iii) 
External Environment. For Power Departments, a 
subset of metrics with modified weightages has been 
adopted from the overall methodology to ensure 
relevance and fairness in assessment.
	
The ratings were carried out by Deloitte Touche 
Tohmatsu India LLP, a reputed consulting firm, and 
were co-ordinated by your Company. These ratings 
serve as valuable diagnostic tools in the hands of the 
State Governments as well as Utilities to leverage their 
strengths and address areas requiring improvements 
so as to improve their operational efficiency and 
financial sustainability.
	
The Fourteenth Integrated Ratings for FY2024–25, 
covering 65 power distribution utilities across 
the country, were released by the Hon'ble Union 
Minister of Power and Housing & Urban Affairs on 
January 23, 2026.
ii.	
Annual Performance Report of Power Utilities
	
PFC has been publishing the Report on Performance 
of Power Utilities annually. The Report covers State 
Power Utilities in all states and UTs and major private 
distribution companies, offering a comprehensive 
insight into the Indian power sector. The Report covers 
a range of key financial and operational parameters 
such as profitability, gap between average cost of 
supply and average revenue, net worth, receivables, 
payables, AT&C losses and consumption pattern 
of the sector at utility, state and national level. The 
Report is part of PFC’s effort to provide a reliable 
database on the performance of power utilities 
offering critical inputs for policy interventions and 
monitoring the progress of various GoI schemes in 
the power sector. The Report for FY2024-25 has been 
published in February 2026.

15.	 Right to Information: Empowering Citizens 
through Transparent Communication
	
The Right to Information Act, 2005 (RTI Act) 
provides citizens with a statutory framework to 
access information held by public authorities, 
thereby promoting transparency, accountability, 
and good governance in public administration. 
The Act reinforces the principles of openness and 
responsible decision-making by enabling citizens 
to seek information on matters concerning public 
authorities, subject to the exemptions prescribed 
under the Act.
	
The RTI Act serves as an important instrument 
for enhancing transparency in the functioning of 
public authorities, fostering accountability of public 
officials, and empowering citizens to participate 
more effectively in the democratic process. It 
has strengthened public oversight by facilitating 
informed engagement from citizens, civil society, 
journalists, and other stakeholders on matters of 
public interest. The preamble of the RTI Act notes 
to secure access to information under the control of 
public authorities, in order to promote transparency 
and accountability in the working of every public 
authority. The information seekers, have, subject 
to few exceptions, an overriding right under the 
Act, to get information lying in the possession of the 
Public Authorities.
	
PFC has set up an elaborate mechanism to deal with 
requests received under the RTI Act, 2005. PFC has 
implemented the RTI Act to provide information to the 
citizens of India and also to maintain accountability 
and transparency in the working of the Company. The 
Company has designated a Public Information Officer 
(PIO) and a First Appellate Authority-RTI (FAA-RTI) at its 
registered office for effective implementation of the 
RTI Act. The relevant information/disclosures are also 
made available on the official website (www.pfcindia.
co.in) of the Company. During the period from April 01, 
2025 to March 31, 2026, all 125 applications received 
under the RTI Act, were duly processed and replied 
to. PFC has also complied with the requirement of 
filing of online RTI Quarterly Returns on the portal 
of Central Information Commission (CIC) during the 
said period.
	
Further, in order to strengthen compliance of the 
provisions of disclosures as contained in Section 4 of 
the RTI Act, 2005, Department of Personnel & Training 
(DoPT) vide its OM No. 1/6/2011-IR dated 15.04.2013 
issued guidelines on the following:-
	
(i)	
Suo moto disclosure of more items under 
Section 4;
	
(ii)	 Guidelines for digital publication of proactive 
disclosure under Section 4;
	
(iii)	 Guidelines for certain clauses of Section 4(1)(b) 
to make disclosure more effective;
	
(iv)	 Compliance mechanism for suo-moto disclosure 
(proactive disclosure) under RTI Act, 2005.
	
In compliance of the aforesaid Guidelines, PFC has 
placed the requisite information on the website of 
the Company.
	
Besides the above, PFC is also linked with the online 
RTI Portal of Govt. of India, Department of Personnel 
& Training (https://rtionline.gov.in), which enables 
citizens of India, to file RTI applications/first appeals 
online along with payment gateway. Payment 
can be made through internet banking of SBI & its 
associate banks, debit/credit cards of Master/Visa 
and RuPay cards.

trajectory during FY 2025–26, supported by sustained 
investments in generation capacity, transmission 
infrastructure, distribution reforms, and renewable 
energy development. The sector remains a key 
enabler of India's economic growth, with increasing 
electricity demand driven by industrial expansion, 
urbanisation, digitalisation, and the transition 
towards cleaner sources of energy. Renewable 
energy has emerged as a major contributor to the 
country's installed power capacity, reflecting India's 
commitment to achieving its clean energy and net-
zero objectives. Continued capacity additions in 
solar, wind, hydro, and energy storage systems, along 
with the modernisation of the national transmission 
network, have strengthened grid reliability and 
facilitated greater integration of renewable energy

implementation of smart metering, advanced digital 
technologies, and distribution sector reforms has 
enhanced operational efficiency, improved billing 
and collection mechanisms, and strengthened the 
financial sustainability of power utilities.

on universal access to electricity, expansion of 
transmission infrastructure, energy efficiency 
initiatives, Green Energy Corridors, and the 
Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) has 
created significant investment opportunities across 
the power value chain. These policy initiatives, 
coupled with the growing focus on battery energy 
storage systems, green hydrogen, electric mobility, 
and smart grid technologies, are expected to drive 
long-term capital expenditure in the sector.

opportunities to support investments across 
generation, renewable energy, transmission, 
distribution, energy storage, and emerging clean 
energy technologies. The increasing participation 
of private sector developers, public sector utilities,

projects is expected to sustain strong demand for 
long-term project financing, refinancing, and 
innovative financial solutions. The Indian power sector 
is well positioned for sustained growth, supported 
by stable policy initiatives, increasing private 
investments, technological advancements, and rising 
electricity demand. The continued transition towards 
a resilient, low-carbon, and digitally enabled power 
ecosystem is expected to strengthen the sector's 
investment potential and reinforce its critical role 
in achieving India's long-term economic and energy 
security objectives. As a leading infrastructure 
financing institution, the Company remains well 
positioned to capitalise on these opportunities 
by providing timely, innovative, and sustainable 
financing solutions that support the country's energy 
transition and infrastructure development.

while supporting India's transition to a low-carbon and 
energy-secure economy.
Indian Carbon Market- Carbon Credit Trading Scheme 
(CCTS): The Ministry of Power has operationalised 
the Indian Carbon Market through the Carbon Credit 
Trading Scheme (CCTS), creating a framework to 
incentivize greenhouse gas emission reductions 
and promote low-carbon investments. The scheme 
comprises both compliance and voluntary offset 
mechanisms, enabling industries to meet emission 
intensity targets while fostering the generation and 
trading of carbon credits. This initiative is expected 
to accelerate India's transition to a low-carbon 
economy, strengthen climate action, and support the 
development of a robust domestic carbon market.
India targets 500 GW of non-fossil fuel power capacity 
by 2030, making Battery Energy Storage Systems 
(BESS) essential for integrating renewable energy 
and ensuring reliable electricity supply. The National 
Electricity Plan 2023 estimates a requirement of 208 
GWh of BESS by 2030. To promote energy storage, the 
government has introduced policy reforms, financing 
support, market mechanisms, Viability Gap Funding 
(VGF) schemes for about 43 GWh of BESS, and a H18,100 
crore PLI scheme for battery manufacturing. Currently, 
India has 798 MWh of operational BESS capacity and 
35.8 GWh under construction, supporting the country's 
clean energy transition and grid reliability goals.
Pump Storage Projects (PSP): India has an estimated 
pumped storage potential of about 258 GW, of which 
nearly 7 GW has been developed so far. To support the 
growing integration of renewable energy and enhance 
grid stability, the Government has set a target of 
adding 57 GW of pumped storage capacity by 2031-32. 
Of this, around 12 GW is under construction, while the 
remaining capacity is at various stages of development.

•	 Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) 
& Smart Metering:
The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), 
launched by the Government of India in 2021, 
continues to be one of the most significant reform 
initiatives aimed at improving the operational 
efficiency, financial sustainability and service 
quality of power distribution utilities (DISCOMs). 
The scheme seeks to modernise the distribution 
network through infrastructure strengthening, 
digitalisation and smart metering, while improving 
the financial health of DISCOMs by reducing 
Aggregate Technical & Commercial (AT&C) losses 
and bridging the gap between the Average Cost of 
Supply (ACS) and Average Revenue Realised (ARR).
The  scheme encompasses comprehensive distribution 
reforms, including network modernisation, feeder 
segregation, High Voltage Distribution Systems (HVDS), 
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA), 
Distribution Management Systems (DMS) and large-
scale deployment of Advanced Metering Infrastructure 
(AMI). Consumer-centric initiatives such as prepaid smart 
metering, rebates, check meters and simplified arrear 
recovery mechanisms have further accelerated smart 
meter adoption and improved billing efficiency.

India's power generation sector, driven by capacity 
expansion, diversification of energy sources, and 
initiatives to strengthen energy security. During the

by accelerated additions in renewable energy and

fuel sources, including 274.68 GW of renewable 
energy and 8.78 GW of nuclear power. This marks a 
significant milestone in India's energy transition, with 
non-fossil sources accounting for more than half of 
the country's installed electricity capacity.

non-fossil capacity, led by 44.61 GW of solar power 
and 6.05 GW of wind power. Solar energy remained

demand, successfully serving a peak demand of

national energy shortage of only 0.03%.

project implementation, enhanced transmission 
infrastructure, and growing private sector 
participation. India also achieved the milestone of 
50% cumulative installed electricity capacity from

ahead of its 2030 target under the Paris Agreement.

expanding capacity to achieve 500 GW of non-fossil 
electricity capacity by 2030, strengthening energy 
security while advancing the country's transition to 
a reliable, resilient, and sustainable power system.

Transmission
	
The transmission sector continued to expand 
with a focus on strengthening grid infrastructure, 
improving reliability and facilitating renewable 
energy evacuation. The Government finalised the 
National Electricity Plan for Transmission (2023–2032) 
to support future electricity demand, including a 
projected peak demand of 458 GW by 2032. The plan 
envisages an investment of approximately H9.16 lakh 
crore for development of transmission infrastructure.
	
Under the planned expansion, the transmission 
network is expected to increase from 4.98 lakh 
circuit kilometres (ckm) in November 2025 to 6.48 
lakh ckm by 2032, while transformation capacity 
is projected to rise from 1,398 GVA to 2,345 GVA. 
Inter-regional transfer capacity is planned to increase 
from 120 GW to 168 GW, enabling efficient transfer of 
electricity across regions and supporting renewable 
energy integration.

while advancing India's transition towards a secure, sustainable, and Iow—carbon energy future.

to the transmission system, including 6,511 ckm

objective of building a financially viable, efficient, and 
consumer-oriented power distribution ecosystem.

Natural capital refers to the ecosystem services and 
environmental resources that businesses depend on 
or impact, including biodiversity, ecosystem health, 
air, water, land, minerals, and forests. Sustainable 
management of natural capital helps ensure regulatory 
compliance, mitigate environmental risks, and align 
business operations with ecological sustainability goals.
PFC is committed to environmental protection by 
minimizing the consumption and wastage of natural 
resources. Through digitalisation and IT-enabled 
solutions, the company continues to reduce paper usage 
wherever possible. As a financial institution, PFC has 
limited scope for recycling waste and materials; however, 
it has installed an Organic Composting machine at its 
office premises to manage organic waste generated from 
the kitchen, pantry, and other areas. By reducing paper 
dependency, PFC supports employees in adopting more 
sustainable and low-carbon work practices.
PFC continues to promote responsible business 
practices through initiatives that support resource 
efficiency, environmental stewardship, and workplace 
sustainability. The Company remains committed to 
contributing to national sustainability objectives by 
integrating environmental considerations into its 
operations and financing activities.
With a vision of accelerating India’s net-zero ambitions, 
PFC continues to play a pivotal role in financing renewable 
energy projects and supporting the country’s clean 
energy transition. The gross loan assets recorded a 
growth of 6.81%, I5,80,115 crore as on March 31, 2026 
from I5,43,120  crore as on March 31, 2025.
Through its continued investments in renewable energy 
and sustainable development, PFC enhances and 
preserves natural capital while aligning its business 
strategy with India’s climate goals and the principles of 
responsible economic growth.

institutional framework, reinforcing its commitment to ethical 
conduct, transparency, accountability and excellence in its 
conduct. As a Maharatna Central Public Sector Enterprise,

governance, ensuring that its affairs are directed and managed 
with integrity, fairness and responsibility while safeguarding 
the interests of all stakeholders. The Company’s governance 
framework is designed to foster prudent decision-making, 
effective risk management, regulatory compliance and 
sustainable value creation, reinforcing stakeholder confidence 
and supporting the nation’s development priorities through 
responsible business practices.
The Company is dedicated to complying with the principles 
governing disclosures and statutory obligations, thereby 
ensuring the protection of shareholders’ rights, equitable 
treatment of stakeholders, timely and transparent 
disclosures, accountability, responsibility and sustainability. 
PFC consistently endeavors to uphold and implement its 
corporate governance philosophy in both letter and spirit.
At PFC, corporate governance represents a commitment to 
conducting business ethically and responsibly within the 
existing regulatory framework, with a strong emphasis on 
sustainable value creation for stakeholders. It also focuses 
on nurturing and maintaining effective relationships 
among the Board of Directors, management, shareholders, 
employees, customers, and other stakeholders.

Remuneration Policy
The Company is a Central Public Sector Undertaking (CPSU), 
wherein all members of the Board of Directors are appointed by 
the President of India through the administrative Ministry, i.e., 
the Ministry of Power, Government of India. The remuneration 
of the Whole-Time Directors is determined by the Government 
of India and specified in their respective appointment orders/
pay fixation orders. The appointment and remuneration of 
other employees of the Company are governed by the applicable 
guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises 
(DPE). Except for the remuneration received by the Chairman 
& Managing Director (CMD) and Whole-Time Directors, none 
of the Directors on the Board has any material pecuniary 
relationship or transactions with the Company, its Promoters, 
or its Subsidiary, which, in the opinion of the Board, may affect 
the independence of judgment of the Directors.
Being a Government Company, the performance evaluation 
of all members of the Board, including Independent 
Directors, is undertaken by the administrative Ministry, 
i.e., the Ministry of Power, Government of India, in 
accordance with the applicable Government guidelines.
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) vide its 
notification dated June 05, 2015 has inter-alia exempted 
the Government Companies in case the Directors are 
evaluated by the Ministry or Department of the Central 
Government which is administratively in charge of 
the Company, as per its own evaluation methodology. 
Accordingly, PFC being a Government company is 
exempted in terms of above notification as the evaluation 
of performance of all the members of the Board including 
Independent Directors is undertaken by administrative 
ministry i.e. Ministry of Power, Government of India.
Further, MCA vide Notification dated July 05, 2017 
prescribed that the provisions relating to review of 
performance of Independent Directors and evaluation 
mechanism, prescribed in Schedule IV of the Companies 
Act, 2013, is also not applicable to Government Companies.
However, the said requirements are still not exempted 
under the SEBI (Listing Obligation & Disclosures 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 for government 
Companies. Accordingly, a draft evaluation policy has 
been referred to Ministry of Power seeking guidance in 
the matter, who has in turn further referred the said draft 
policy to the CPSE policy division for further examination.
In the meantime, to comply with Regulation 17(10) SEBI 
LODR, the Board of Directors in its meeting held on 
15.04.2026 evaluated the performance of Independent 
Directors. During evaluation, the concerned Independent 
Director abstain himself/herself from the participation.
The evaluation of Non-Independent Directors for the 
FY2025-26 was carried out by Independent Directors 
in their meeting held on 14.04.2026 in compliance of 
SEBI LODR.

C.	 A brief on the type of customers	
PFC is a leading financial institution that provides interest-bearing financial assistance to entities across the power 
sector. Its client base includes Central and State power utilities, private sector power utilities including independent 
power producers, joint sector power utilities, as well as power equipment manufacturers and companies engaged 
in infrastructure and logistics.
PFC offers a comprehensive suite of financial products comprising long-term, medium-term, and short-term loans, 
designed to address the diverse financing requirements of the power sector across its value chain. The Company supports 
the development, modernization, expansion, and operational needs of power infrastructure projects by extending financial 
assistance to Central and State utilities, State Governments, independent power producers, and other eligible entities. 
Through its financing solutions, PFC contributes significantly to strengthening and sustaining India's power infrastructure.

Yes. The Company has established a comprehensive Code of Business Conduct and Ethics that provides guidance on 
ethical conduct, including the identification, disclosure, and management of conflicts of interest involving the Board

a. 	
Whether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? 
(Yes/No). If yes, the coverage such system? 	
	
PFC is committed to promoting the physical, mental, and overall well-being of its employees by fostering a safe, 
healthy, and supportive work environment. The Company adopts a holistic approach to employee wellness through 
regular health awareness programmes, capacity-building initiatives, preventive healthcare services, and occupational 
health and safety measures.
	
During FY 2025–26, PFC conducted a series of training and awareness programmes focused on employee well-
being and workplace safety. These included workshops on Health and Stress Management, Yoga and Mindfulness, 
Occupational Health and Safety Management Systems (ISO 45001:2018), and specialised training for Internal Quality 
Auditors in accordance with ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 45001:2018 standards.
	
To strengthen preventive healthcare, the Company organized five medical camps across its Offices providing 
employees with access to essential health screening and medical consultation services. In addition, daily virtual 
yoga sessions are conducted to encourage physical fitness, mental well-being, and work-life balance.
	
The Corporate Office is equipped with a dedicated medical facility staffed by qualified practitioners from multiple 
disciplines, including Allopathy, Ayurveda, Gynaecology and Homoeopathy ensuring employees have access to 
professional healthcare during working hours. A Wellness Centre is also available to provide first aid and emergency 
medical assistance whenever required.
	
Through these initiatives, PFC continues to strengthen its culture of health, safety, and employee well-being while 
promoting a resilient, productive, and engaged workforce.
b.	
What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-
routine basis by the entity?	
	
PFC has established a structured framework to identify, assess, and mitigate workplace health and safety risks, 
ensuring a safe and secure working environment for its employees. The Company regularly conducts fire safety 
training, emergency evacuation drills, and fire safety awareness programmes to strengthen employee preparedness 
and reinforce a culture of safety.
	
The workplace is equipped with clearly visible fire safety signage, strategically located fire extinguishers, and advanced 
fire detection, smoke sensing, and burglar alarm systems to enable timely response during emergencies. In addition, 
electronic surveillance and real-time alert monitoring systems are deployed to continuously monitor the premises 
and facilitate the early identification of potential safety hazards.
	
Through these preventive measures and continuous monitoring, PFC remains committed to maintaining high 
standards of occupational health and safety while fostering a safe, resilient, and risk-aware workplace.
c.

from such risks. (Y/N)	
	
PFC has a Safety Officer responsible for overseeing surveillance, access controls, sensors, and fire safety systems to 
ensure premises security.

Yes. PFC provides Group Personal Accident Insurance coverage to all employees and workers. The Company also 
offers access to medical facilities, including medical rooms at its premises, and conducts regular physical and mental 
well-being programmes to support the overall health and wellness of its workforce.

PFC identifies its key stakeholder groups through a structured stakeholder engagement and materiality assessment 
process. Stakeholders are identified based on their influence on the organization, dependence on PFC's operations 
and financing activities, and the extent to which they are impacted by the Company's business decisions.

assessments to understand stakeholder expectations and prioritize key ESG issues.

customers/borrowers, suppliers and vendors, employees, and communities as its key stakeholder groups.

stakeholder outreach, and public accessibility to its advocacy and thought leadership initiatives.

About this report
Statement of use
Power Finance Corporation Limited (PFC) is pleased to present 
its third Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Report 
for FY 2025-26, titled “Financing a Greener India”.
This year's report marks a significant step forward 
in our sustainability reporting journey. Building on 
the foundation laid in our previous ESG reports, 
we have further strengthened our disclosures by 
aligning the report with the recommendations 
of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial 
Disclosures (TCFD) and the Sustainability Accounting 
Standards Board (SASB) frameworks, while 
continuing to report in reference to the Global 
Reporting Initiative (GRI) Universal Standards 
2021. With this, PFC's ESG reporting is now aligned 
with three internationally recognised reporting 
frameworks, reflecting our continued commitment 
to transparent, comprehensive and globally aligned 
sustainability disclosures.
As India advances towards its ambitious Net Zero 
target by 2070, PFC continues to be a key catalyst in 
enabling the low-carbon transition across the power 
and infrastructure sectors, sectors that remain 
central to building a resilient, sustainable economy. 
This ESG report serves as a strategic communication 
tool, offering our stakeholders a clear and 
comprehensive view of our ESG performance, 
key initiatives and long-term commitments. It 
has been prepared in alignment with the eight 
GRI foundational reporting principles,  accuracy, 
balance, clarity, comparability, completeness, 
sustainability context, timeliness and verifiability 
— supporting consistent, high-quality sustainability 
reporting that enables stakeholders to track PFC’s 
progress across our environmental, social and 
governance priorities. 
Previous editions of our ESG report are accessible 
on our corporate website (https://pfcindia.co.in/en/
pages/investors/esg-report).
Reporting period and 
frequency
This third ESG report presents PFC’s ESG 
performance for the reporting period from 1st April 
2025 to 31st March 2026.
Reporting scope and 
boundary
The ESG disclosures in this report are primarily 
focused on PFC’s standalone operations, covering 
ESG practices across governance, lending activities 
and internal business functions. 
The report captures our direct operational impacts, 
with particular emphasis on our role in supporting 
India’s clean energy transition through the strategic 
financing of clean energy projects. It also reflects 
our continued commitment to social responsibility, 
including our efforts toward community 
development and inclusive growth.
The material ESG topics covered in this report were 
identified through a stakeholder engagement 
and materiality assessment exercise conducted 
in March-April 2024, spanning both internal and 
external stakeholders. There has been no change 
to the material topics disclosed in our previous ESG 
reports.

CMD Message
Dear Stakeholders,
India's energy sector is at an important point 
in its evolution. The challenge today is not only 
to add generation capacity, but to build an 
energy system that is reliable, affordable and 
increasingly clean. 
As India's largest power sector financier, PFC 
has a unique responsibility in supporting this 
transition by directing capital towards projects 
that strengthen energy security while advancing 
the country's sustainability goals.
This report reflects how that responsibility 
continued to evolve during FY 2025–26.
In recent years, global developments have 
repeatedly reminded us that sustainability 
cannot be viewed as a separate agenda. For a 
financial institution like us, it is reflected in the 
choices we make every day, what we finance, 
how we assess risks, the partnerships we 
build and the long-term impact our financing 
creates. The assets we finance today will 
continue to serve the nation for decades. 
That is why every financing decision we make 
carries a responsibility that extends far beyond 
the balance sheet. Responsible financing is 
therefore not an additional responsibility for 
PFC; it is central to our mandate.
This belief continued to guide us during FY 
2025–26. Over the past year, we expanded our 
support beyond conventional renewable energy 
financing to areas that will shape the next 
phase of India's energy transition. Our financing 
portfolio now includes battery energy storage 
systems, pumped storage projects, green 
hydrogen and domestic manufacturing across 
the clean energy value chain. These investments 
will play an important role in strengthening 
India's energy ecosystem.
Our financing priorities continue to remain 
closely aligned with the Government of India's 
vision for a secure, resilient and sustainable 
energy future. Today, PFC is one of India's 
leading financiers of renewable energy, having 
supported over 66 GW of renewable energy 
capacity.
A key milestone during the year was the first 
comprehensive impact assessment of PFC's 
commissioned renewable energy portfolio 
(excluding large hydro). As a financial institution, 
our greatest environmental contribution lies not 
in our own operations, but in the projects we 
enable. For the first time, we have measured the 
environmental impact of our renewable energy 
financing, providing a clearer understanding 
of the emissions avoided through the projects 
we support. The assessment shows that our 
outstanding commissioned renewable energy 
portfolio of 10.6 GW is estimated to avoid 
approximately 10.39 million tonnes of CO2 
emissions annually. We believe this marks an 
important step in measuring the outcomes of 
our financing, rather than only reporting the 
capital deployed.
We also strengthened the framework that 
supports our sustainable financing activities. 
During the year, PFC updated its Green Bond 
Framework in line with the latest internationally 
recognised principles, further enhancing 
transparency for investors and reinforcing our 
access to global sustainable finance markets. 
At the same time, we continued to deepen 
our engagement with leading government

About PFC
Power Finance Corporation Limited (PFC), a 
Maharatna Central Public Sector Enterprise 
under the Ministry of Power, Government of 
India, is the country’s leading Non-Banking 
Financial Company (NBFC) in the power sector. 
Incorporated in 1986 and classified as an 
Infrastructure Finance Company by the Reserve 
Bank of India, PFC has been at the forefront of 
financing India's power sector for nearly four 
decades. Through its financing support across 
generation, transmission, distribution and 
renewable energy segments, PFC has played a 
pivotal role in the development of India’s power 
infrastructure. Backed by this sectoral expertise 
and operational excellence, PFC continues to 
serve as a strategic financial partner to both 
public and private sector entities, delivering 
customised financing solutions calibrated to 
their investment needs.
In recent years, PFC has significantly expanded 
its focus on renewable energy and clean 
technology financing, in step with India’s climate 
goals, while demonstrating strong financial 
resilience and prudent risk management 
across a diversified loan portfolio. PFC’s vision 
is to be the ‘leading institutional partner for 
the power and allied infrastructure sectors 
in India and overseas across the value chain’. 
Through its ESG-aligned initiatives, robust 
governance practices and enduring stakeholder 
partnerships, PFC remains committed to 
enabling a sustainable, self-reliant and resilient 
energy future for India.

through efficient asset utilisation, responsible 
resource management, and prudent operational 
practices.

FY 2025-26 marked a major milestone in 
PFC’s climate reporting journey. For the first 
time, PFC assessed the climate impact of its 
entire commissioned renewable energy 
portfolio (excluding large hydro) outstanding 
as on 31 March 2026.
This study covered over 100 commissioned 
RE projects with aggregate funded capacity of 
10.6 GW across solar, wind, hybrid, waste-to-
energy and small hydro projects (excluding 
Large Hydro). The assessment provides a 
comprehensive view to date of the emissions 
avoided through our financing activities.
Financing Clean Energy. 
Enabling Decarbonisation.
The commissioned renewable energy portfolio 
assessed is estimated to avoid approximately 
10.39 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions every 
year—equivalent to removing 2.26 million 
passenger vehicles from the road annually.
The scale of these avoided emissions 
demonstrates how long-term financing can 
contribute to decarbonisation by enabling 
renewable energy infrastructure across India.
Our Financed Impact Far Exceeds Our 
Operational Footprint
While PFC’s operational Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions 
were 1,257 tCO₂e during FY 2025-26, the commissioned 
renewable energy assets financed by the Company are 
estimated to avoid 10.39 million tCO₂e annually.
This highlights that our Scope 1 and 2 provides a limited 
measure of our environmental performance and our 
larger impact lies in the renewable energy projects we 
finance, where financing enables emissions reductions 
at scale. Together, these efforts reinforce PFC’s role in 
supporting India’s clean energy transition and long-term 
Net Zero 2070 ambition.

Key assumptions used 
in the assessment are 
as follows:
1.	 Emission Factors:
The baseline emission factor is based 
on the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) 
of India’s emission factors Version 22.0 
(2025), applying the Combined Margin 
emission factor of 0.738 tCO2/MWh as 
specified in CDM Tool 07 Version 7.0. This 
factor represents the emissions intensity 
of grid electricity that would otherwise 
have been generated from conventional 
sources.
2.	 Generation Data:
The portfolio maintains high data quality 
standards with more than 80% of the 
funded projects reporting actual available 
generation data. For the remaining 
projects, emissions avoided were 
conservatively estimated using CEA-
standard capacity utilisation factors- 21% 
for solar, 25% for wind projects and 30% 
for hybrid, ensuring robust climate impact 
calculations.
3.	 Attribution Approach:
A project-specific attribution factor was 
applied to each project to reflect PFC’s 
proportional financing contribution to 
total project cost. This is aligned with 
the Partnership for Carbon Accounting 
Financials (PCAF) Part A methodology 
for project finance attribution and with 
the GHG Protocol Scope 3, Category 15 
principles for financed emissions and 
avoided emissions assessment.

role as a catalyst for India’s clean energy 
transition. Going forward, PFC will continue 
to support India’s Panchamrit goals, 
including the ambition to expand non-fossil 
fuel-based capacity, reduce the emissions 
intensity of the economy and progress 
towards long-term net-zero commitments, 
while continuously enhancing the 
transparency and robustness of its climate 
impact reporting.

India’s Energy Financing Ecosystem
India’s energy and ﬁnancial sectors continue to exhibit gender disparities, particularly
in workforce participation and leadership roles. Within the energy sector, women
remain underrepresented, especially in technical and project-related functions.
In May 2025, a comprehensive gender assessment study was conducted by Frankfurt
School of Finance & Management in partnership with KfW (Kreditanstalt für
Wiederaufbau) as part of the preparatory work for a new line of credit to PFC.
The study aimed to evaluate gender inclusion at PFC, identify structural gaps, and
recommend targeted interventions aligned with international ESG and development
ﬁnance expectations. Against this backdrop, we aimed to strengthen gender equality,
diversity, and women’s empowerment across our organization—while embedding
gender inclusion within our ﬁnancing and governance approach.

Ensuring Pay Parity
Our commitment to equitable treatment begins 
with how we value and compensate our people. 
We ensure equal remuneration to men and 
women employees in accordance with the Equal 
Remuneration Act, 1976 with no discrimination 
based on gender. Being a government 
undertaking, employee pay, and allowances 
are determined according to guidelines issued 
by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), 
Ministry of Finance, Government of India. These 
pay guidelines are applicable to all CPSEs in a 
grade-wise manner without any gender-based 
disparities.
Equal Opportunity Policy:
This policy affirms our commitment to a 
fair and inclusive workplace by prohibiting 
discrimination based on religion, race, caste, 
gender, or place of origin. It promotes equal 
access to recruitment and career advancement 
opportunities and ensures equal pay for equal 
work, in accordance with Government of India 
guidelines and the Equal Remuneration Act, 
1976.
Fair representation of marginalised sections:
To ensure adequate representation of 
marginalized sections, various safeguards, 
relaxations, and concessions are available for 
employees belonging to Scheduled Castes (SC), 
Scheduled Tribes (ST), Other Backward Classes 
(OBC) categories (socially and economically 
disadvantaged sections of society, as 
designated by the Government of India) and 
Persons with Disabilities.
The Economically Weaker Section (EWS) 
from the general category is provided with 
a 10% reservation, in line with government 
guidelines. A Special Reservation Cell, aided 
by Liaison Officers, Recognized SC/ST/OBC 
Welfare Associations and an internal grievance 
redressal system address community-specific 
concern. Various selection committees 
for recruitment and promotion include 
representatives from SC/ST, OBC, minority and

and effective resolution of employee issues.

Our Board of Directors functions as an apex 
decision-making body and is supported by 
various sub-committees across key domains 
such as audit, investment, human resources, 
CSR and enterprise risk management. Board 
meetings and meetings of the board level

Board of Directors
Our Board of Directors comprises experienced 
professionals with expertise across finance, 
the power sector, policy and regulation, risk 
oversight, and corporate governance, enabling 
balanced guidance on our strategic priorities 
and long-term direction.
In accordance with Article 86 of our Articles 
of Association and PFC being a government 
company under the Companies Act, 2013, all the 
directors on the board of PFC are appointed by 
the Government of India. The Board comprises 
the Chairman & Managing Director, Functional 
Directors, a Government Nominee Director 
and Independent Director(s). Being a CPSE, the 
Functional Directors are appointed through 
a selection process guided by the principles 
of merit, transparency and compliance with 
the guidelines issued by the Department of 
Public Enterprises (DPE). The Public Enterprises 
Selection Board (PESB), a government authority, 
carries out the appointment process, including 
issuance of advertisement for the vacancy,

Board Tenure
The tenure of Directors on PFC’s Board is shaped 
by three broad rules sets: The Companies 
Act. 2013, the SEBI (LODR) Regulations 2015 
(Listing Regulation) and the Department of 
Public Enterprises (DPE) guidelines for Central 
Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). These 
frameworks, together with Ministry of Power 
(MoP) appointment orders, determine how long 
each category of Director may serve and the 
conditions for re-appointment or cessation.
PFC’s whole time Directors, including the 
Chairperson & Managing Director (CMD) and 
the Functional Directors are appointed by 
the Government of India for a maximum of 
five years or until the incumbent’s date of 
superannuation, whichever is earlier.
Part time Non-Official (Independent) Directors 
are governed by Section 149(10) – (11) of the 
Companies Act. 2013 and Regulation 17(1A) of 
the SEBI LODR Regulations, which together cap 
their service at two consecutive terms of up to 
five years each (an overall ceiling of ten years), 
after which requires a three-year cooling-off 
period. DPE’s corporate governance guidelines 
for listed CPSEs mirror this philosophy, 
prescribing an initial three-year term that may 
be extended based on performance for another 
three years for Independent Directors, and a 
Board composition of at least 50% independent 
Directors once the CPSE is listed and having 
executive Chairman.
Board Committees
To enable focused oversight and efficient 
decision-making, we have constituted nine 
Board-level committees covering areas such 
as audit, risk, CSR, and IT governance. Each 
committee operates under a defined mandate 
and includes a mix of Functional Directors and 
Independent Directors, supporting balanced 
deliberation and specialized supervision.
This committee-led oversight approach also 
supports stronger institutional alignment 
between our strategic objectives, internal 
controls, and regulatory expectations. As 
governance priorities continue to evolve, this 
structure provides an effective mechanism for 
monitoring emerging risks, reviewing control 
effectiveness, and strengthening accountability 
across our key business functions.

Grievance Redressal 
Mechanism
We recognise grievance redressal as an essential 
component of good governance, stakeholder 
responsiveness, and ethical business conduct. 
To support the fair and timely resolution of 
concerns, we have established a structured, 
multi-tier grievance framework covering both 
internal and external stakeholders, including 
employees, vendors, shareholders, customers, 
and the public. This system promotes openness, 
strengthens confidence in our institutional 
processes, and supports a culture of 
constructive resolution
Our grievance architecture includes dedicated 
channels such as employee grievance cells, 
shareholder communication platforms, 
vendor support systems, and customer service 
interfaces, each designed to address concerns 
with procedural clarity and objectivity.

charges, loan terms, covenant interpretation, and policy-related matters.

handled through the GeM Incident Management System for quick grievance resolution.

of borrower grievances and improving service

strengthen timely resolution of concerns while

To ensure broader public accountability, PFC 
also facilitates redressal through the following 
platforms:
•	
PIDPI (Public Interest Disclosure and 
Protection of Informers): Complaints 
against PFC lodged through PIDPI are 
handled by a designated independent 
government body, being the Central 
Vigilance Commission (CVC). This is an 
offline as well an online portal wherein the 
complaints can be lodged 24X7.

Redress and Monitoring System): 
CPGRAMS portal is connected to PFC. The 
status of public grievances is available on

stakeholders.

In compliance with the RTI Act, PFC has 
designated its Company Secretary as Public 
Information Officer (PIO) to review and 
respond to RTI applications. Further, an 
Executive Director level officer has been 
designated as a First Appellate Authority 
(RTI) in PFC to review RTI appeals.
•

Grievance Redressal Portal: PFC has also 
established an Online Grievance Redressal 
Portal, including a dedicated Borrower 
Grievance Portal, to enable borrowers to 
raise concerns and seek timely resolution 
through a structured and accessible digital 
mechanism.

that all grievances, whether internal or 
external - are addressed fairly, promptly, and in

Vigilance – promoting 
transparency and 
accountability
Our vigilance function serves as a cornerstone 
of our governance framework, driving ethical 
conduct, transparency, and institutional 
integrity. Headed by the Chief Vigilance Officer 
(CVO), appointed by the Government of India, 
our vigilance unit operates under the oversight 
of the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 
and focuses on three core areas: preventive 
vigilance, punitive vigilance, and surveillance and 
detection.

(FY 2025–26)
PFC observed Vigilance Awareness campaign in 
line with the guidelines of the Central Vigilance 
Commission (CVC). This observance formed 
part of a preventive vigilance campaign focused 
on strengthening systems, promoting ethical 
conduct, and enhancing transparency across our 
organisation. During FY 2025–26, PFC observed 
Vigilance Awareness Week from October 27 to 
November 2, 2025, across its corporate and 
regional offices, as part of the Central Vigilance 
Commission’s three-month Preventive Vigilance 
Campaign. The Week was observed under the 
theme “Vigilance: Our Shared Responsibility” 
and focused on strengthening systems and 
controls, promoting ethical conduct, enhancing 
transparency and accountability, and building  
a culture of integrity.
The observance commenced with the 
administration of the Integrity Pledge to 
employees, including through the e-Integrity 
Pledge available on PFC’s intranet portal. 
Various awareness activities were organised, 
including slogan writing, poem writing and 
pictorial competitions, along with a workshop 
on “Vigilance Angle.” At the valedictory function 
held on October 30, 2025, PFC unveiled the third

Regulatory Compliance
We remain committed to embedding regulatory 
compliance within our wider governance and 
risk management framework. In alignment 
with the requirements of authorities such 
as RBI, SEBI, and the Ministry of Power, we 
have instituted a structured compliance 
control system supported by an independent 
compliance function, periodic audits, regular 
assessments, and reporting to senior leadership 
and the Board. This system helps us identify 
gaps, facilitate corrective action, and mitigate 
legal, financial, and reputational risks.
To foster a strong compliance culture, PFC has 
a dedicated Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), 
who is responsible for overall oversight in 
ensuring adherence to applicable regulatory 
requirements for NBFCs. The CCO is responsible 
for monitoring compliance risks, and compliance 
testing to determine the organisation 
compliances with legal/regulatory requirements, 
risks and control framework.
Further strengthening governance, PFC has 
an independent Internal Audit function that 
serves as a critical pillar of its risk management 
framework. This function provides independent 
assurance that the organization’s risk 
management, governance and internal control 
processes are operating effectively. PFC has a 
Board approved Risk Based Internal Audit (RBIA) 
framework in place in line with RBI regulations.
By integrating regulatory compliance with 
vigilance, risk oversight, and awareness-
building, we continue to strengthen institutional 
assurance, procedural discipline, and trust in 
our governance systems.

BRIEF OUTLINE ON CSR POLICY OF THE COMPANY
	
PFC’s has formulated its CSR Policy in line with Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (CSR) 
Rules, 2014 (as amended from time to time) and DPE guidelines issued from time to time. The aim of PFC’s Corporate 
Social Responsibility Policy (CSR Policy) is to ensure that the Company becomes a socially responsible corporate 
entity committed to improving the quality of life of society at large by undertaking projects for Sustainable 
Development, mainly focusing on Health, Education and Energy needs of the society. To oversee the activities of 
CSR, PFC has in place a Board level CSR Committee of Directors headed by an Independent Director. Every year 
CSR Annual Action Plan and Budget are recommended by CSR Committee and approved by the Board. Third party 
impact assessment agencies are being engaged to assess the benefit/outcome of the projects. 
	
PFC has implemented wide range of activities throughout the Country in the field of Environment Sustainability, 
Healthcare, Education, PM Internship, Rural Development, contribution to Swachh Bharat Kosh and other areas

Fair Valuation of Derivative financial instruments 
The Company enters into derivative contracts 
in accordance with RBI guidelines to mitigate its 
currency and interest rate risk in accordance with 
currency risk management policy approved by the 
Board of Directors of the Company.
Derivative contracts are either categorized at 
Fair Value through P&L (FVTPL) or under cash 
flow hedge (Hedge Accounting). Mark to market 
gain/loss on derivatives categorized at FVTPL is 
recognized in Statement of Profit and Loss and that 
of Hedge Accounting is recognized in the Other 
Comprehensive Income. 
We consider the valuation of the derivative financial 
instruments and hedge accounting as a key audit 
matter due to material exposure and the fact that 
the inappropriate application of these requirements 
/assumptions/estimate by contracting bank could 
lead to a material effect on the income statement.
[Refer Note No. 41 and 40.4 to the Standalone 
Financial Statements read with Note No. 5.3.3]
Our audit procedures included: 
The Company has availed services of an independent expert for 
preparation of a model for derivative accounting as per Ind AS 109. 
Discussed with management to have an understanding of its 
perception and also reviewed policy of the Company for risk 
management. 
Evaluated key internal controls over classification of derivative 
instruments. 
The Company obtains fair value of derivative from the counterparty 
banks as on the reporting date, which are relied upon by us. Our 
procedure included evaluation of details of various financial 
derivative contracts outstanding as on March 31, 2026 and fair 
value thereof.
Additionally, we verified the accounting of gain or loss on mark to 
market basis of derivative contracts in Statement of Profit & Loss 
and Other Comprehensive Income in case of derivatives contracts 
under cash flow hedge.
Based on the aforesaid procedure, we have reviewed accounting of 
derivatives in the books of account and assessed that the related 
disclosures are given in the financial statements.

Our objectives are to obtain reasonable assurance 
about whether the Standalone Financial Statements as 
a whole are free from material misstatement, whether 
due to fraud or error, and to issue an auditor’s report 
that includes our opinion. Reasonable assurance 
is a high level of assurance, but is not a guarantee 
that an audit conducted in accordance with SAs will 
always detect a material misstatement when it exists. 
Misstatements can arise from fraud or error and are 
considered material if, individually or in the aggregate, 
they could reasonably be expected to influence the 
economic decisions of users taken on the basis of 
these Standalone Financial Statements.
	
As part of an audit in accordance with SAs, we exercise 
professional judgment and maintain professional 
skepticism throughout the audit. We also:
•	 Identify and assess the risks of material misstatement 
of the Standalone Financial Statements, whether 
due to fraud or error, design and perform audit 
procedures responsive to those risks, and obtain 
audit evidence that is sufficient and appropriate 
to provide a basis for our opinion. The risk of not 
detecting a material misstatement resulting from 
fraud is higher than for one resulting from error, 
as fraud may involve collusion, forgery, intentional 
omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of 
internal control.
•	 Obtain an understanding of internal control relevant 
to the audit in order to design audit procedures 
that are appropriate in the circumstances. Under 
section 143(3)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013, we 
are also responsible for expressing our opinion 
on whether the Company has adequate internal 
financial controls system in place and the operating 
effectiveness of such controls.
•	 Evaluate the appropriateness of accounting 
policies used and the reasonableness of 
accounting estimates and related disclosures made 
by management.
•	 Conclude on the appropriateness of management’s 
use of the going concern basis of accounting and, 
based on the audit evidence obtained, whether a 
material uncertainty exists related to events or 
conditions that may cast significant doubt on the 
Company’s ability to continue as a going concern. 
If we conclude that a material uncertainty exists, 
we are required to draw attention in our auditor’s 
report to the related disclosures in the Standalone 
Financial Statements or, if such disclosures are 
inadequate, to modify our opinion. Our conclusions 
are based on the audit evidence obtained up to the 
date of our auditor’s report. However, future events 
or conditions may cause the Company to cease to 
continue as a going concern.
•	 Evaluate the overall presentation, structure and 
content of the Standalone Financial Statements, 
including the disclosures, and whether the 
Standalone Financial Statements represent the 
underlying transactions and events in a manner that 
achieves fair presentation.
	
Materiality is the magnitude of misstatement in the 
Standalone Financial Statements that, individually or 
in aggregate, makes it probable that the economic 
decisions of a reasonably knowledgeable user of the 
Financial Statements may be influenced. We consider 
quantitative materiality and qualitative factors in (i) 
planning the scope of our audit work and in evaluating 
the results of our work and (ii) to evaluate the effect 
of any identified misstatements in the Financial 
Statements.
